fetched_contents.text: A comprehensive diagnostic approach to detect underlying causes of obesity in adults Summary Obesity is a worldwide growing problem. When confronted with obesity, many health care providers focus on direct treatment of the consequences of adiposity. We plead for adequate diagnostics first, followed by an individualized treatment. We provide experience‐based and evidence‐based practical recommendations (illustrated by clinical examples), to detect potential underlying diseases and contributing factors. Adult patients consulting a doctor for weight gain or obesity should first be clinically assessed for underlying diseases, such as monogenetic or syndromic obesity, hypothyroidism, (cyclic) Cushing syndrome, polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), hypogonadism, growth hormone deficiency, and hypothalamic obesity. The most important alarm symptoms for genetic obesity are early onset obesity, dysmorphic features/congenital malformations with or without intellectual deficit, behavioral problems, hyperphagia, and/or striking family history. Importantly, also common contributing factors to weight gain should be investigated, including medication (mainly psychiatric drugs, (local) corticosteroids, insulin, and specific β‐adrenergic receptor blockers), sleeping habits and quality, crash diets and yoyo‐effect, smoking cessation, and alcoholism. Other associated conditions include mental factors such as chronic stress or binge‐eating disorder and depression.Identifying and optimizing the underlying diseases, contributing factors, and other associated conditions may not only result in more effective and personalized treatment but could also reduce the social stigma for patients with obesity. Keywords: Diagnostics, genetic obesity, hormones, medication, secondary causes 1. INTRODUCTION Obesity (body mass index [BMI] ≥30.0 kg/m2) is a chronic disease1 that is a worldwide growing problem.2 In 2015, over 603 million adults had obesity, and 4.0 million deaths were yearly accountable to a high BMI.3 When facing a patient with obesity, most clinicians focus on treating the associated comorbidities and/or simply recommend weight loss. The diagnostic phase, which is typically used when assessing other clinical problems, is often overlooked in obesity. Whereas in other clinical problems, such as hypertension, clinicians are alert to consider a wide variety of secondary causes.4 For obesity, a diagnostic phase to detect underlying diseases or other factors that hinder weight loss is recommended by some5 but not all clinical practice guidelines. The European guideline recommends a diagnostic phase; however, specific examples of diseases or factors that may contribute to obesity are lacking.5 Others do not mention the necessity to identify underlying contributing factors.6, 7 This paper aims to help clinicians to deepen the diagnostic phase with a comprehensive overview of possible contributors to weight gain for an individual. Currently, on a societal level, it is widely believed that obesity is simply the consequence of overconsuming unhealthy foods and lack of exercise. However, on an individual level, there are many other contributing factors or underlying diseases, which are often not identified and may prove significantly associated with weight gain and barriers to weight loss. We suggest that clinicians should first detect and address underlying diseases and contributing factors, before starting obesity treatment. Besides lifestyle‐related factors, other factors include hormonal and genetic abnormalities, mental and socio‐cultural factors, and side effects of medications. Identifying these underlying factors may lead to more personalized treatment strategies, can also increase patients' understanding of their obesity, and reduce their social stigma. 1.1. Clinical presentation 1.1.1. Clinical Case A A 66‐year‐old man, known with type 2 diabetes mellitus and eczema, was referred because of obesity. Since the last decade, he became increasingly heavier, with a rapid weight gain of 30 kg in the last year. He noticed red striae under his armpits and suffered from mood swings and decreased libido. A detailed past medication list showed several episodes of using clobetason cream, triamcinolone, desoximetason, and one short course of prednisone in the last 8 years. Moreover, in the last year, he had used large amounts of mometason cream on his whole back and arms because of severe eczema. We saw a man weighing 168 kg (BMI 59.5 kg/m2) with pronounced abdominal obesity with purple striae, hematomas, and severe non‐pitting ankle edema. Laboratory results are shown in Table 1. We concluded that there was severe obesity, with multiple contributing causes: an exogenous Cushing syndrome due to the use of large amounts of dermal corticosteroids, late‐onset hypogonadism (which can be a consequence of obesity but also poses an opportunity for treatment8), and non‐pitting lymphedema. The subclinical hypothyroidism was considered a consequence of obesity.9, 10 A multidisciplinary strategy comprised gradual tapering of topical corticosteroids and lymphedema compression therapy by his dermatologist, testosterone supplementation, and an exercise program. After 2 years, he had lost 35 kg, his clinical condition improved, and testosterone and TSH levels had normalized. fetched_contents.text: The reality of menopause weight gain The hormonal changes of menopause tend to make it more likely that women will gain weight around the abdomen, rather than the hips and thighs. But hormonal changes alone don't necessarily cause the weight gain. Instead, it's usually related to aging, as well as lifestyle and genetic factors. For example, muscle mass typically goes down with age, while fat increases. Losing muscle mass slows the rate at which the body uses calories. That rate is called metabolism. This process can make it more difficult to stay at a healthy weight. If you continue to eat as you always have and don't do more physical activity, you're likely to gain weight. Most people become less active as they age. Paying attention to your activity and trying to move more may help keep you at a healthy weight. Genetic factors also might play a role in weight gain around menopause. If your parents or other close relatives carry extra weight around the abdomen, you probably will too. Other factors, such as eating a diet that isn't healthy and not getting enough sleep, might contribute to menopause weight gain. When people don't get enough sleep, they tend to snack more and eat and drink more calories.

How to assess and quantify the patient’s weight change

A clinician should start by asking about weight history and timing because weight gain is often best understood as a pattern rather than a single moment. The evidence says that unexplained weight gain is when a person gains pounds without increasing food intake or decreasing physical activity, and that causes range from aging and hormonal changes to health conditions and medications [N2-R2]. It also emphasizes that clinicians should first assess underlying diseases and contributing factors, including medication, sleep habits, crash diets, smoking cessation, alcoholism, chronic stress, and binge-eating disorder [N2-F1]. That makes timing and context central to the evaluation: when the weight change started, how quickly it happened, and whether it coincided with lifestyle changes, stress, or other triggers.

For a patient who does not know exact pounds gained, the interpretation is more cautious. The evidence notes that a comprehensive diagnostic approach should first detect underlying causes, including medication and contributing factors, rather than assuming obesity is simply the result of overeating and lack of exercise [N2-F1]. It also says that patients consulting a doctor for weight gain should first be clinically assessed for underlying diseases and contributing factors [N3-R1]. In this case, the patient’s uncertainty about pounds gained does not automatically mean the change is unreal; it may instead reflect a lack of objective tracking, a slow or gradual change, or a perceptual shift that is real but hard to measure precisely [N2-R4]. A clinician should therefore treat the lack of exact numbers as a sign that more careful tracking is needed, not as proof that the patient is imagining the weight gain.

Objective measurements or repeat weight checks are helpful when the patient’s self-report is incomplete. The evidence recommends that clinicians should first detect underlying diseases and contributing factors before starting obesity treatment, and that a multidisciplinary approach may include identifying and optimizing those factors [N2-F1]. Repeat weight checks are especially useful if the patient’s change is rapid enough to be meaningful, because the Cleveland Clinic notes that if you gain 2 to 3 pounds a day or 5 pounds a week, you should see a provider [N3-R2]. However, the evidence also says that unexplained weight gain can be diagnosed by examining medical history, lifestyle, and potential conditions like thyroid issues or diabetes [N3-R3]. That means objective measures are best used in combination with a thorough history, rather than in isolation.

Overall, the clearest approach is: ask when the change started, how it has progressed, whether it is rapid or slow, and whether any lifestyle, medical, or emotional factors may have changed around the same time [N2-F1][N2-R2]. If the patient is uncertain about exact pounds gained, the clinician should ask for approximate ranges, dates, and whether the change is accompanied by other symptoms [N3-R2]. If the change is likely to be slow or subtle, objective measurements and repeat weight checks can help clarify whether a real trend exists [N2-F1][N3-R2]. But if the patient’s report is vague, the most helpful next step is not immediate alarm but a more structured history and assessment [N2-F1].

# What your symptoms may mean

Your main concern is that you feel heavier lately and that your clothes feel tighter. Based on the evidence, this is a common and understandable worry, and it is reasonable to suspect that you may be experiencing a real weight change, especially if the feeling is new and has started recently. However, the evidence also says that weight gain is often not as obvious as inactivity or poor diet, and that many causes are subtle or not dramatic [N1-R5][N2-R2]. That means it is important to think about both real weight gain and other possible explanations before jumping to conclusions.

## 1) Is this likely real weight gain or a perceptual change?

Clothing feeling tighter can be a real sign of weight gain, but it is not by itself strong proof that a large amount of weight has been gained. The evidence says that unexplained weight gain is when you put on pounds without increasing food intake or decreasing physical activity, and that clothes getting tight or the scale going up can be signs of an issue [N1-R3][N1-R2]. It also says that weight gain may stem from causes that are not obvious, and that unexplained weight gain can be diagnosed by examining medical history, lifestyle, and potential conditions [N1-R4][N1-R5]. That means tighter clothes can be real, but they can also reflect changes in body shape, posture, fluid retention, or temporary changes in muscle or water content [N1-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5].

So the most likely answer is: **it is possible you are gaining weight, but the evidence does not yet prove that a large or dramatic gain is occurring** [N1-R5][N2-R2]. The best way to decide is to track the change over time and look for additional symptoms.

## 2) Which symptoms would support a more specific diagnosis?

The evidence points to several clues that could point to a specific cause. The strongest and most relevant pattern is menopause or perimenopause-related weight gain. The Mayo Clinic says menopause-related hormonal changes make women more likely to gain weight around the abdomen rather than the hips and thighs, and that aging, lifestyle, and genetic factors are usually behind the weight gain [N5-F2]. It also says menopause-related stress and poor sleep can raise cortisol, which may lead the body to hold onto fat [N6-R1]. That makes abdominal fat gain, fatigue, changes in sleep, stress, or menstrual changes especially relevant symptoms [N5-F2][N6-R1].

Other symptoms that would support a more specific diagnosis include:
- sudden or rapid weight gain, especially if it is large enough to be noticeable
- fatigue or changes in energy
- changes in sleep or stress
- recent lifestyle changes, such as reduced activity or changes in diet
- other hormonal or metabolic symptoms, such as menstrual irregularities, skin changes, or changes in appetite [N2-F1][N2-R2]

In short, the more specific the symptoms, the better you can narrow down what might be happening.

## 3) What medical conditions are plausibly supported by your report?

The evidence supports several plausible conditions, especially those related to hormonal or metabolic changes.

### Likely explanations
- **Menopause or perimenopause-related weight gain**: this is the most directly relevant condition because menopause tends to increase abdominal fat and is often linked to stress, poor sleep, and hormonal changes [N5-F2][N6-R1].
- **Hormonal changes and stress-related cortisol elevation**: chronic stress can raise cortisol, which may lead to fat retention, especially around the abdomen [N5-F2][N6-R1].
- **Aging and lifestyle changes**: the evidence says that aging, lifestyle, and genetic factors are often behind weight gain [N5-F2].
- **Medication side effects or other reversible factors**: the evidence explicitly notes that medications, stress, sleep, crash diets, smoking cessation, alcoholism, and binge-eating disorder can contribute to weight gain [N2-F1].

### Less urgent or reversible causes to consider first
The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that many causes of weight gain are not as dramatic as obesity alone and that clinicians should first assess underlying diseases and contributing factors [N1-R5][N2-F1]. So the most likely first explanations are usually:
- stress or poor sleep
- changes in activity or routine
- temporary metabolic shifts
- menopause or perimenopause-related changes [N2-F1][N5-F2][N6-R1]

### Conditions not strongly suggested by the report alone
The evidence also says that rare syndromic or monogenetic obesity, Cushing syndrome, PCOS, and other specific conditions are plausibly supported in a broader clinical picture, but they are not strongly suggested by the patient’s report alone [N2-F1]. Those would require more specific symptoms or signs before they are considered.

## 4) How should a clinician assess and quantify your weight change?

A clinician should start by asking about **weight history and timing** because weight gain is best understood as a pattern rather than a single moment [N2-R2][N2-F1]. They should also ask:
- when the change started
- how quickly it has happened
- whether it coincided with any lifestyle, medical, or emotional changes
- whether the patient knows or can estimate how much weight has changed [N2-F1][N2-R2]

For a patient who does not know exact pounds gained, the evidence suggests that the lack of exact numbers does not automatically mean the change is unreal; it may instead reflect a lack of objective tracking, a slow or gradual change, or a perceptual shift that is real but hard to measure precisely [N2-R4][N2-F1]. In this case, the best next step is usually to **track weight and symptoms more carefully** rather than assume the change is dramatic or alarmingly large.

Objective measurements or repeat weight checks are helpful when the change is likely to be slow or subtle, because the Cleveland Clinic says that if you gain 2 to 3 pounds a day or 5 pounds a week, you should see a provider [N3-R2]. The evidence also says that clinicians should first detect underlying diseases and contributing factors before starting obesity treatment, and that a comprehensive diagnostic approach is recommended [N2-F1]. That means objective measures are best used in combination with a thorough history, rather than in isolation.

## 5) What should you do next?

### Practical next steps
If you want to be more certain, the evidence supports:
- **weighing yourself regularly**, ideally at the same time of day and under similar conditions
- **tracking your clothing fit and other symptoms**
- **noting changes in sleep, stress, activity, and diet**
- **keeping a simple journal or log of weight and symptoms** [N3-R2][N3-R3][N2-F1]

The evidence also says that clothing feeling tighter is useful but can reflect fluid retention, muscle gain, or temporary changes in posture and body shape [N1-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5]. So the best approach is to track how the change is progressing and whether it is accompanied by other symptoms.

### When to see a doctor
The evidence suggests you should see a provider if the change is **rapid** or if other symptoms develop. The Cleveland Clinic says if you gain 2 to 3 pounds a day or 5 pounds a week, you should see a provider [N3-R2]. The PMC article also says clinicians should first detect underlying diseases and contributing factors and that a comprehensive diagnostic approach is recommended [N2-F1]. In your case, if the change is slow and you do not have other concerning symptoms, the evidence supports observing at home for a short period while tracking weight and symptoms [N3-R2][N2-F1].

### What to avoid
You should avoid:
- **overinterpreting vague or temporary changes as a serious condition without more evidence**
- **jumping to conclusions about a specific diagnosis**
- **ignoring lifestyle and temporary factors**
- **undertaking unnecessary testing or excessive worry** unless the change becomes rapid or other symptoms appear [N1-R5][N2-F1]

Your symptoms suggest that it is **possible** you are gaining weight, and clothing feeling tighter can be a real sign, especially if it is accompanied by other symptoms such as fatigue, changes in sleep, stress, or abdominal fat gain [N1-R3][N1-R2][N5-F2][N6-R1]. However, the evidence also says that weight gain is often not as obvious as inactivity or poor diet, and that many causes are subtle or reversible [N1-R5][N2-R2]. That means the most reasonable next step is to **track your weight and symptoms carefully** and to see a doctor if the change becomes rapid or if other concerning symptoms appear [N3-R2][N2-F1].

In short:
- **Clothing feeling tighter may be a real sign**, but it is not enough on its own to prove a large weight gain [N1-R3][N1-R2].
- **Menopause or stress-related changes are among the most plausible explanations**, especially if you are in the relevant age range or under recent stress [N5-F2][N6-R1].
- **You should not ignore the change, but you also should not assume the worst** without more evidence [N1-R5][N2-F1].
- **The best next step is to weigh regularly, track symptoms, and seek care if the change becomes rapid or concerning** [N3-R2][N2-F1].

The evidence suggests you should see a provider if the change is **rapid** or if other symptoms develop. The Cleveland Clinic says if you gain 2 to 3 pounds a day or 5 pounds a week, you should see a provider [N3-R2]. The PMC article also says clinicians should first detect underlying diseases and contributing factors and that a comprehensive diagnostic approach is recommended [N2-F1]. In your case, if the change is slow and you do not have other concerning symptoms, the evidence supports observing at home for a short period while tracking weight and symptoms [N3-R2][N2-F1].

### What to avoid
You should avoid:
- **overinterpreting vague or temporary changes as a serious condition without more evidence**
- **jumping to conclusions about a specific diagnosis**
- **ignoring lifestyle and temporary factors**
- **undertaking unnecessary testing or excessive worry** unless the change becomes rapid or other symptoms appear [N1-R5][N2-F1]

## 6) Bottom line

However, the evidence also says that weight gain is often not as obvious as inactivity or poor diet, and that many causes are subtle or reversible [N1-R5][N2-R2]. That means the most reasonable next step is to **track your weight and symptoms carefully** and to see a doctor if the change becomes rapid or if other concerning symptoms appear [N3-R2][N2-F1].
